extracted.intended_audience: authors querying agents or publishers with nonfiction books or memoirs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing query letters (and related submission materials) to agents or publishers for nonfiction projects, including narrative-driven nonfiction (memoir, biography) and information-driven nonfiction. Emphasizes elements to include, platform/market considerations, and common pitfalls to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a finished, polished book proposal (with sample chapter[s])
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you begin the query process: you should have a finished and polished book proposal ready to go, which should include at least one sample chapter, if not more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should be the best you can make it. If you can send the book proposal along with the query, the query functions largely as a cover letter and needn't be labored over. The proposal overview and the query may include similar language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author platform and ability to market
rubrics_metrics.description: Your query and book proposal not only have to present an effective argument for why your book should exist, but also should reflect your authority and platform as a book author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform equates to visibility or ability to sell books. You must quantify and demonstrate reach (e.g., blog visits, newsletter subscribers, media gigs). For information-based nonfiction, platform is especially crucial; without platform muscle, New York publishers are unlikely to be interested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization: where you customize the letter for the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If referred by someone, heard them speak, or read their work, put that up front. Example: mention if vouched for by an existing client or if you heard the agent speak at a conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: What you’re selling
rubrics_metrics.description: What you’re selling: genre/category, anticipated word count, title/subtitle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the category and an estimated word count. Be cautious: word counts much higher than 100,000 may invite rejection; ~80,000 is industry standard for narrative nonfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: Hook (compelling description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hook: a compelling description of the narrative (particularly important for narrative-driven nonfiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with a strong hook that conveys protagonist, conflict, stakes, and the 'sizzle' that makes the story unique. Example opening: 'When I was eighteen years old, I moved from my hometown...' For memoir, write the hook in first person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: Target readership (specific audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Target readership: who will buy this book and why? (it cannot be everyone and anyone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a meaningful, specific audience (e.g., 'the 2 million corporate employees who quit their jobs every month' or 'degree-seeking students in the 500 creative writing programs'). Avoid sweeping claims like 'anyone who has children.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: Your bio, platform and credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Your bio, platform and credentials to write the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include publication credits (name them), relevant professional background, awards/positions, mainstream media attention, ongoing gigs that reach the audience (columns, podcasts), audience size metrics, and any major personalities who will blurb or write a foreword. Self-published work may be mentioned if you can cite strong sales numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query elements: Thank you and closing
rubrics_metrics.description: Thank you and closing: polite sign-off with contact info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close with a thank you and include phone number, e-mail address; no need to detail availability. If sending snail mail, include a self-addressed stamped envelope (SASE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-driven queries should condense proposal overview
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’ve written a book proposal, your query letter is often a more condensed version of your proposal’s overview or summary—those first 500 words (or first one to three proposal pages) should summarize the most important and salable qualities of your book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your query and proposal overview should both answer: (1) So what? (2) Who cares? (3) Who are you?

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer the three core selling questions
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) So what? Why is this book unique, special or needed in the current marketplace? (2) Who cares? Who is the identifiable and specific audience who will spend $20 on this book? (3) Who are you? Why are you the best author for this book—what are your platform and credentials?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the query clearly addresses uniqueness/market need, a specific target audience, and the author's authority/platform. It's acceptable for query and proposal language to overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead first paragraph with your strongest selling point
rubrics_metrics.description: Put your best foot forward—lead with your strongest selling point in the very first paragraph of the query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with personalization, a strong hook, platform/credentials, or a compelling target readership—whichever is your strongest asset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative-driven projects must show story quality and marketability
rubrics_metrics.description: For narrative-driven nonfiction, the writing and storytelling matters as much as it would for a novel, and your hook plays an important role in conveying the quality of the story. The publisher also has to envision a sizable audience for that story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rejections that a project 'reads like an extended magazine article' or that 'the audience is too small.' Boil down story to protagonist + conflict, choices/stakes, and sizzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a narrative hook with protagonist, stakes, and sizzle
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a narrative-driven hook, boil down your story to: Protagonist and her conflict; The choices the protagonist has to make (the stakes); The sizzle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sizzle = what sets your work apart; avoid tired storylines. For memoir, use first person and convey liveliness, voice, and personality—hooks lacking life or voice may fail even if premise is interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tired or overused memoir storylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sizzle means this idea isn’t tired and hasn’t been done a million times before; many memoir topics are saturated (e.g., addiction recovery, generic dysfunctional-family narratives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents look for unique angles or exceptional life experience; avoid clichés like 'I was born in a big/small town, and I liked listening to punk music...' Use concrete, distinctive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-based nonfiction needs a unique selling proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: For information-based nonfiction, nail a unique selling proposition to set your book apart from the competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming the book will be 'the first and only book to do X' is powerful. Describe special features, unique research, proven systems, and clear reader benefits (how readers' lives will improve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and document platform/visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s not enough to say you have visibility—you have to be able to point to it, quantify it, and show how you’re ready to lift off into book sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numbers (e.g., website visits, newsletter subscribers), ongoing visibility channels (columns, podcasts), and concrete indicators of reach. Weak platform increases the need for an irresistible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a meaningful and appropriately sized target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Most authors go too broad when identifying the target audience; the target must be specific and actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague or universal audiences and meaningless statistics (e.g., 'Google returns 152 million results'). Use defensible audience estimates and comparable titles to indicate market size; be realistic about 'Goldilocks' size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use competitive/comp titles carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing to other titles similar to your own can help convey target audience, but avoid citing the latest bestseller or movie-tied title as a lazy comp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comparisons like 'the next Eat, Pray, Love'—agents are tired of reductive comps. Use comps that accurately reflect readership or positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to mention in your bio (specific items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your bio should include publication credits, relevant professional background, recognition or awards, national/mainstream media attention, ongoing gigs, the size of your current audience, and major personalities who will blurb the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about credits (don’t say 'a variety of journals'). If self-published, mention sales only if proud and prepared to discuss results; otherwise omit until necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate query length
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate length for a nonfiction query is somewhere between 1 and 1.5 pages, single spaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually the shorter, the better. If sending the full proposal, the query can be shorter since it acts as a cover letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred and risky word counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighty thousand words is the industry standard for a narrative nonfiction work; book’s estimated word count much higher than 100,000 may court rejection before an agent reads the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information-based nonfiction varies tremendously, but high word counts are a red flag to most publishers and agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous querying and batch strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t have to state that you are simultaneously querying. In today’s environment, everyone assumes this. Do not request exclusivity; send queries out in batches of three to five—or more if confident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author does not need to declare multiple queries. Exclusive queries are not recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mention query history or editorialize quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t mention your 'history' with the work (e.g., how many agents you’ve queried, near misses, compliments). Resist the temptation to editorialize—don’t proclaim how much the agent will love it or that it will be a bestseller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show your writing quality rather than telling. Also don’t criticize your work in the letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact, availability, and meeting etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s no need to go into great detail about when/how you’re available. Put contact info at the bottom (phone and e-mail). Do not introduce the idea of an in-person meeting with the agent or editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you know you'll hear them speak at a conference, you may mention looking forward to hearing them, but don’t ask for a meeting. Use official conference channels to set appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up and silence as response
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often complain they never receive a response. Sometimes silence is the new rejection; send one follow-up to inquire if necessary, but don’t keep sending emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that lack of response may be a form of rejection. One polite follow-up is permitted; repeated messages are discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website listing and no body-of-query prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: List your website as part of your contact info, but there's almost never any need to tell agents in the body of the query to visit your website for more info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents will Google you anyway; avoid instructing them to check your site in the letter body.
